findings.current: the descendants of the Xianbei ruled Liaoning Province
findings.defect: The Korean calls the Xianbei descendants the dominant power in Liaoning Province; it does not establish that they ruled the province.
findings.rationale: 패자 means the hegemon or dominant power in a region, not necessarily its formal ruler.
findings.replacement: the descendants of the Xianbei were the dominant power in Liaoning Province

findings.current: Some of those who filled the vacuum there included informants from the Hebei Peng Family.
findings.defect: The assembled English omits the description of the newcomers as new kinds of people not previously seen on the grasslands.
findings.rationale: The source explicitly describes the people entering the long-lawless grasslands as new human groups before identifying the Peng Family informants among them.
findings.replacement: New kinds of people, never before seen on the grasslands. Some of those who filled the vacuum there included informants from the Hebei Peng Family.

findings.defect: This turns a forceful shout into a verbal command meaning to stop. The Korean is a shouted exclamation, not an instruction to end something.
findings.rationale: 갈(喝) is a cry or shout here, accompanying the release of his power; it does not mean “Enough.”

findings.current: Men born on the open plain who died in the saddle.
findings.defect: The past-tense “died” makes this sound like a description of particular men, rather than the source’s general characterization of the horse-riding people.
findings.rationale: The Korean uses a generic present-tense contrast: they are born on the plain and die on horseback.
findings.replacement: Men born on the open plain who die in the saddle.

summary: The assembled English is largely faithful, but it shifts a regional power description, omits a source image, and changes two details of the battle scene.
